title: IdentiFlight stops wind turbines when it detects eagles at a Wyoming wind farm; estimates of the cut in eagle deaths range from 50% to 82% and are disputed
summary: Researchers estimated an 82% (75%–89%) relative cut in eagle deaths at a Wyoming wind farm after IdentiFlight began curtailing turbines; two federal statisticians later put it at 50% (−159%, 89%).
account: McClure et al. tested an automated curtailment system at the Top of the World Windpower Facility in Wyoming, United States. The authors are from The Peregrine Fund, Western EcoSystems Technology and the U.S. Geological Survey. The system's cameras detect and classify flying objects, and the system curtails individual turbines. The design was before–after–control–impact, with a control site 15 km away. Recharge reported the claim on 28 January 2021. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor logged the 82% result as a positive record. The study appeared in the Journal of Applied Ecology (Crossref publication date 31 January 2021). Correcting for carcass detection probability, the authors estimated that fatalities fell 63% at the treatment site (95% confidence interval 59%–66%). Fatalities rose 113% at the control site. Relative to the control site, this is an 82% (75%–89%) reduction. The authors noted that fatalities were not eliminated. On 26 August 2022 the same authors reported in Ecological Solutions and Evidence that, with additional data from the same site, eagle fatalities fell by 85% (95% highest density interval 12% to 100%). Duerr et al. (PLoS One, 26 January 2023) assessed an IdentiFlight installation in California. The system correctly identified 77% of eagles and 85% of non-eagles. It issued 5,439 virtual curtailment orders for non-eagle targets against 850 for eagles. These orders did not slow the turbines. Huso and Dalthorp (Journal of Applied Ecology, 30 August 2023) reanalyzed the Wyoming data and reported four major errors. They reported that the corrected data give 50% (−159%, 89%), consistent with no effect. McClure et al. replied the same day that their data support the efficacy of automated curtailment. In its final eagle permit rule of 12 February 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service answered comments that asked for IdentiFlight in permit conditions. The Service said that permittees may use such technologies but that their efficacy has not been studied enough to require them.
purpose: IdentiFlight is built to detect and classify flying eagles and curtail individual turbines to avoid collisions; reduced eagle fatalities are the intended outcome.
system: IdentiFlight automated eagle detection and turbine curtailment (camera system with machine-learning classification)
deployer: Top of the World Windpower Facility, Wyoming

ratings.reason: McClure et al. report that eagle fatalities at the treatment site fell by 63% after automated curtailment, a measurable improvement in a conservation result. They state that deaths were not eliminated. Two U.S. Geological Survey statisticians reanalyzed the data and put the effect at 50%, with an interval that includes an increase, so the size of the effect is disputed.

ai_role.statement: The system's classification decisions trigger curtailment, so any fatality reduction runs through the AI. The peer-reviewed estimate is independent of the maker but is challenged by a peer-reviewed reanalysis (50%, interval including zero). The California assessment shows 23% of eagles missed and six times more virtual orders for non-eagles than for eagles; these orders did not slow the California turbines. The size of the benefit is therefore unsettled.

data.answer:
Peregrine Fund, WEST and USGS researchers estimated an 82% (75%–89%) relative cut in eagle deaths at a Wyoming wind farm after IdentiFlight curtailment; a 2023 reanalysis put it at 50% (−159%, 89%).

The mortality estimate is contested across the original analysis, reanalysis, rebuttal, and later confirmation. Their assumptions and uncertainty intervals must be reconciled before selecting one headline percentage. The California classification study also raises missed-eagle and unnecessary-curtailment concerns.

fields.account: McClure et al. tested an automated curtailment system at the Top of the World Windpower Facility in Wyoming, United States. The authors are from The Peregrine Fund, Western EcoSystems Technology and the U.S. Geological Survey. The system's cameras detect and classify flying objects, and the system curtails individual turbines. The design was before–after–control–impact, with a control site 15 km away. Recharge reported the claim on 28 January 2021. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor logged the 82% result as a positive record. The study appeared in the Journal of Applied Ecology (Crossref publication date 31 January 2021). Correcting for carcass detection probability, the authors estimated that fatalities fell 63% at the treatment site (95% confidence interval 59%–66%). Fatalities rose 113% at the control site. Relative to the control site, this is an 82% (75%–89%) reduction. The authors noted that fatalities were not eliminated. On 26 August 2022 the same authors reported in Ecological Solutions and Evidence that, with additional data from the same site, eagle fatalities fell by 85% (95% highest density interval 12% to 100%). Duerr et al. (PLoS One, 26 January 2023) assessed an IdentiFlight installation in California. The system correctly identified 77% of eagles and 85% of non-eagles. It issued 5,439 virtual curtailment orders for non-eagle targets against 850 for eagles. These orders did not slow the turbines. Huso and Dalthorp (Journal of Applied Ecology, 30 August 2023) reanalyzed the Wyoming data and reported four major errors. They reported that the corrected data give 50% (−159%, 89%), consistent with no effect. McClure et al. replied the same day that their data support the efficacy of automated curtailment. In its final eagle permit rule of 12 February 2024, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service answered comments that asked for IdentiFlight in permit conditions. The Service said that permittees may use such technologies but that their efficacy has not been studied enough to require them.

ratings.reason: McClure et al. report that eagle fatalities at the treatment site fell by 63% after automated curtailment, a measurable improvement in a conservation result. They state that deaths were not eliminated. Two U.S. Geological Survey statisticians reanalyzed the data and put the effect at 50%, with an interval that includes an increase, so the size of the effect is disputed.
No source reports a realized outcome for the operator, such as a permit, a cost or a legal risk avoided.
